messages.author: 15bf7097fdc57cf5
messages.subject: 3-dimensional graphs in the future
parts:
Dear all,

I have read the ggplot2 book and there are a couple of hints that indicate a possible development of three-dimensional graphs in ggplot2. I do not want to seem like I am unappreciative of the beautiful 2-d graphs, but I am so curious that I can't help but ask:

Will 3-d capabilities be developed?
Will they be incorporated into ggplot2, or would there be a different package/syntax?

Is there any timetable?

Thank you so much for all of the incredible work that has been done.

Octavio Huertas

messages.author: 52e73b2030a3e651
messages.subject: Re: 3-dimensional graphs in the future
parts:
Hi Octavio, 

I cannot speak for Hadley or any other ggplot2 contributors, but at one point I thought I saw a post or comment from Hadley that 3D plots were not a priority.  Alternatives exist, though:

Have you looked into RGL?  It is not as conceptually/ideologically consistent as ggplot2, but it allows for a great deal of interactive 3D visualization without a lot of work.  If you combine it with Rpanel, it can allow for enormous flexibility in data visualization.  But at that point, you may want an interface which anticipates some needs, and ggobi may be handy.

Rggobi has a good deal to offer -- if you look at Hadley's "clusterfly" and "classifly" packages, both are written against Rggobi and use it for the interface.  It is quite powerful. For example, if you want to look for outliers or swapped samples in a microarray experiment, feeding the principal components to rggobi allows for rapid exploratory analysis.  Likewise for comparisons between batches/operators, and visualizing population substructure in genome-wide association studies.  Most people who try it find they like it.

Between those two packages I find that I very rarely have an unmet need for 3D in ggplot2.

All of the above is written from the standpoint of "well, these get stuff done NOW", so if that's not your desire or intent, please excuse my off-topic response.  It "Would Be Nice" to have 3D ggplot2, but the other packages mentioned above are somewhat complementary IMHO.

Best regards, and I hope this is helpful to you and/or others on the list.

--tim

> Between those two packages I find that I very rarely have an unmet need for

Same here. I'm not terribly interested in 3d graphics because in my
mind there are two interested groups of graphics:

* 2d, the natural dimensionality of our screens and paper
* nD, which we need to by combining multiple graphics or
sophisticated uses of animation

That said, it wouldn't be impossible for someone to come along and
implement ggplot2 (or something similar) on top of RGL, but to me it's
a lot of work for not a lot of gain.

messages.subject: Re: 3-dimensional graphs in the future
parts:
On Tue, Feb 9, 2010 at 15:25, hadley wickham <h.wi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Same here.  I'm not terribly interested in 3d graphics because in my
> mind there are two interested groups of graphics:
>
>  * 2d, the natural dimensionality of our screens and paper
>  * nD, which we need to by combining multiple graphics or
> sophisticated uses of animation

I think this is true for "statistical" graphs (which ggplot is clearly
geared towards), i.e. graphs in which the x, y, (z, w, etc.) position
is just a way to convey the value of a variable, just as colour or
size on the graph. In such cases, even when you have a multivariate
data set, you usually want to summarize it in 2D indeed, for clarity.

However, one situation where I think 3D is meaningful (possibly
unavoidable) is "spatial" plots, in which x, y, and z are actual
spatial coordinates (e.g. lon, lat, altitude). A typical use case for
a 3D-ggplot would be "plot points at the locations of observation of a
particular plant species on a mountain slope and color the points
according to the amount of flowers on each plant". Of course these
graphs could also be projected in 2D, by representing altitude/depth
in another way (size, colour, etc) but they map more naturally to 3D
representations. The use case presented above is of course doable in
RGL, but the syntax is much less natural and consistent than in
ggplot.

JiHO
